clue.text: A university moving sculpture outside to car

indicators.note: the A, U and moving sculpture pieces sit around the word to, so they are outside it

parts.note: a mobile is a hanging sculpture that moves in the air, as made by Calder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A university's kinetic sculpture is being carted outside to a waiting car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' is the container signal: the pieces before it wrap round the plain word 'to', and Calder's hanging artworks supply the moving sculpture.
explanation.definitionFit: An automobile is a motor vehicle, the formal word for a car.

clue.text: A very black English priest in France

parts.note: BB marks a very black pencil lead, blacker than B

explanation.surface: A dark-clad English cleric is living in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Pencil grades run from H (hard) to B (black); BB is extra black.
explanation.definitionFit: Abbé is the French title for a clergyman, especially a secular priest.

clue.text: Home sweet home for The Three Sisters?

definitions.text: Home sweet home for The Three Sisters?

parts.words: Home sweet home for The Three Sisters?
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland the Dormouse tells of three sisters who lived at the bottom of a well of sweet syrup

explanation.walkthrough: The Three Sisters suggests Chekhov's play, but these are the Dormouse's sisters in Alice, living in a well of sweet syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dormouse's sisters lived in a well of this syrup, a literally sweet home.

clue.text: French maid, say, on island in the river

definitions.note: the definition stands for a French form of address, a noun, as in a French young lady

indicators.note: say means the word maid is spoken and spelt as it sounds

parts.note: maid is said exactly like the word made

indicators.note: in puts the island's letter inside the river

parts.note: the Moselle is a river flowing through France, Luxembourg and Germany

explanation.surface: A French maid is spotted on an island in the middle of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French maid' reads as one phrase, but 'maid, say' is a sound-alike and 'French' alone is the definition; 'in' signals the island going inside the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Mademoiselle is the French title for an unmarried woman, the equivalent of Miss.

clue.text: Curious bear cub starting to explore range in 7

indicators.note: curious means odd, so the letters of bear cub are made strange by rearranging
starting to picks the first letter of explore

explanation.surface: An inquisitive young bear sets off to explore the open range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious' rearranges BEAR CUB into BARBECU; E starts 'explore'. 7 is OPEN AIR, so this is an outdoor cooking range.
explanation.definitionFit: A grill used outdoors is a cooking range set up in the open.

clue.text: Unprofessional for students to hold up a foreign agency

indicators.note: to hold means the students' letters go round the other piece

parts.note: L is the learner sign, and two learners give LL

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the piece is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency, foreign from a British viewpoint

explanation.surface: Amateur students are said to be stalling a foreign agency.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reverses the A and the agency, and 'to hold' wraps the two learners round them; L-plates mark learner drivers in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Laical means lay, belonging to ordinary people rather than the clergy or a profession.

clue.text: Egyptian Christian caught talking

indicators.note: talking means the word for caught is said out loud and spelt as it sounds

parts.note: copped is slang for caught, as in copped by the police

explanation.surface: An Egyptian Christian is overheard chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: COPPED, slang for caught, is pronounced the same as COPT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Copts are the native Christian church of Egypt, one of its oldest communities.

clue.text: Outdoor characters in opera

indicators.note: characters means the letters themselves, taken and rearranged

explanation.surface: Some singers perform an opera outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means the letters of IN OPERA, rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-air event takes place outside rather than under a roof, so it is outdoor.

clue.text: Humour capable of being made more acceptable

definitions.text: Humour capable of being made more acceptable

parts.note: temper means mood or humour, as in good temper
able means capable

explanation.surface: A joke that could be toned down to be more palatable.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb, temper means to moderate or make acceptable, so the whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be tempered can be softened or moderated into a more palatable form.

clue.text: Loaf by, say, a lotus tree in the S. Sea Islands

definitions.text: tree in the S. Sea Islands

parts.note: a loaf is a portion of bread
the lotus of legend is a fruit, so 'say' marks it as an example of fruit

explanation.surface: A loaf beside a lotus suggests a picnic under South Sea palms.
explanation.walkthrough: The lotus of Homer's lotus-eaters was a fruit; 'say' signals an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The breadfruit is a Pacific tree, made famous by Captain Bligh's voyage to Tahiti to collect it.

clue.text: Consider giving back the reward

indicators.note: giving back tells us to read the word for reward from right to left

parts.note: meed is an old word for a deserved reward

explanation.surface: Someone weighs up whether to return a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving back' turns MEED, an archaic word for a reward, into DEEM.
explanation.definitionFit: To deem is to judge or hold an opinion, so it is a synonym of consider.

clue.text: Basin in kitchen where you find cheeses

parts.note: a bowl is a basin
taken as written
a galley is the kitchen on a ship or aircraft

explanation.surface: A mixing bowl in the kitchen next to where the cheese is kept.
explanation.walkthrough: In skittles, the heavy disc thrown at the pins is called a cheese, so the alley is where you find them.
explanation.definitionFit: Skittle alleys use flat wooden discs called cheeses, so an alley for skittles is where they are found.

clue.text: Supplied originally with a dirty film

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the word Supplied

parts.note: cum is Latin for with, as in a bedroom-cum-study

explanation.surface: Something was delivered coated in a grimy layer.
explanation.walkthrough: S from 'Supplied originally', then CUM, the Latin word for with that English uses in phrases like house-cum-office.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is a layer of dirt or froth floating on a surface, a grimy film.

clue.text: Welcome back Parliamentary leader, speak, then fade away

indicators.note: back says the Latin greeting for welcome is read in reverse

parts.note: ave is the Latin greeting hail or welcome

indicators.note: leader picks out the first letter of Parliamentary

parts.note: to orate is to speak formally, as in a speech

explanation.surface: An MP is welcomed back, makes a speech, then quietly drifts out of politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns AVE into EVA; then P, the leader of 'Parliamentary', and ORATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that evaporates turns to vapour and vanishes, so the word means to disappear gradually.

clue.text: The skill required to produce both the tattoo and the uniforms

definitions.text: The skill required to produce both the tattoo and the uniforms

parts.words: The skill required to produce both the tattoo and the uniforms
parts.note: a tattoo is pricked into skin with a sharp point, and uniforms are sewn, so both need work with a sharp threaded pin

explanation.walkthrough: A tattoo also means a military display, which suggests uniforms; here it is inked skin, made with a needle.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewing and embroidery are crafts done with a needle, as is tattooing taken literally.

clue.text: Runners about to return weary but with honour

indicators.note: about means the runners go round the other piece

parts.note: emus are big flightless birds that run fast instead of flying

indicators.note: to return says the word for weary is read backwards

parts.note: to tire is to grow weary

explanation.surface: Athletes come back tired but honoured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runners' suggests athletes but means flightless birds; 'to return' reverses the word for weary and 'about' wraps the birds round it.
explanation.definitionFit: An emeritus professor has retired but keeps the title as an honour.

clue.text: Girl's name (not applicable for a queen)

indicators.note: for here means in place of, so the queen's name is shown without the abbreviation

parts.note: Gloriana was the poetic name for Queen Elizabeth I in Spenser's Faerie Queene
N/A is the standard abbreviation for not applicable, written NA

explanation.surface: A form notes that a girl's name is not relevant when applying as a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: GLORIANA, Spenser's name for Elizabeth I, loses NA, the abbreviation for 'not applicable'. The bracket reads as a form-filler's note.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloria is a common female first name, from the Latin for glory.

clue.text: A degree of sickness

parts.note: the phrase reads as an amount of illness, but means a university award granted to a student too ill to sit the exams

explanation.walkthrough: 'Degree' reads as an amount, but it is an academic degree; the Latin word means 'he is sick'.
explanation.definitionFit: An aegrotat is an unclassified university degree granted to someone too ill to take the final examinations.

clue.text: Evasive character of 19

parts.note: the cross-reference points to the author at 19, whose pickpocket in Oliver Twist is known as the Artful one, and an evasive person is also called this

explanation.walkthrough: 19 is DICKENS; the Artful Dodger is the young pickpocket in Oliver Twist, and a dodger is anyone who evades duties.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodger is someone who evades obligations, and the Artful Dodger is the boy thief in Oliver Twist.

clue.text: Devil for an author

definitions.meaning: a euphemism for the devil, as in 'what the deuce'
the Victorian novelist who wrote Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: Someone substitutes the devil for a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old euphemism for the Devil ('what the dickens?') and the surname of the novelist Charles.

clue.text: Name Anatole is strange for a new arrival

indicators.note: is strange tells us the letters of Anatole appear in an odd, unfamiliar order

explanation.surface: Parents find Anatole an odd name to give a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: N, then 'is strange' rearranges ANATOLE into EONATAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Neonatal means relating to the first weeks of a baby's life, so it describes care for a newborn.

clue.text: Cyclone gets the Navy into trouble

annotationWithheld.why: Cyclone gets the Navy into trouble: the Navy gives RN, but no clue word gives the TO + ADO that would surround it; 'into' would have to be split into an indicator and letters
annotationWithheld.clue: Cyclone gets the Navy into trouble

clue.text: These bones sound harder

indicators.note: sound tells us the word for harder is spoken and spelt as it is heard

parts.note: sterner means harder or more severe

explanation.surface: Some bones are said to be tougher than others.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech STERNER and STERNA sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterna is the plural of sternum, the breastbone, so the word names several such bones.

clue.text: Powered flight may be in store for you

definitions.text: Powered flight may be in store for you

parts.words: Powered flight may be in store for you
parts.note: a flight here is a set of stairs, and a motorised one is found in a department store

explanation.walkthrough: 'Powered flight' suggests aircraft and 'in store' suggests the future; the flight is of stairs, and the store is a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving staircase carries shoppers between floors, a staircase run by a motor.

clue.text: Wary crook

indicators.note: crook as a verb means to bend, so the letters of Wary are bent out of shape

explanation.surface: A suspicious criminal keeps an eye out.
explanation.walkthrough: Bend ('crook') WARY to get the answer; the whole clue also hints at the sense, crook being Australian slang for wrong or broken.
explanation.definitionFit: Awry means askew or gone wrong, like something bent out of true.

clue.text: A little dusky lady, akin to a Malaysian

indicators.note: a little means only a small part of the words dusky lady, akin is taken

explanation.surface: A dark-skinned woman is said to resemble someone from Malaysia.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'laDY AKin'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dyaks are indigenous peoples of Borneo, part of which lies in Malaysia.

clue.text: Duck by the German river

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, written as O
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: A duck swims beside the German river.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is a zero score in cricket, hence O; DER is German for 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oder is a central European river forming much of the border between Germany and Poland.

clue.text: Spotted butterfly in flower

definitions.meaning: a family of orange butterflies with dark chequered markings
a bulb plant with chequered bell-shaped blooms, the snake's head

explanation.surface: A speckled butterfly settles inside a bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the lily-family plant and the butterflies are named for their chequered, dice-box markings.

clue.text: Helen's immortaliser

parts.note: in Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, Faustus asks Helen of Troy to make him immortal with a gesture of the lips

explanation.walkthrough: Marlowe's line is 'Sweet Helen, make me immortal with a kiss.' The clue reverses who does the immortalising.
explanation.definitionFit: In Faustus's speech a single touch of lips is what grants immortality.

clue.text: Former train chef won't run out of puff

parts.note: past means former, as in past times
RY is an abbreviation for railway, standing in for train
a cook is a chef

explanation.surface: An ex-railway cook still has plenty of breath left.
explanation.walkthrough: Puff is puff pastry here, not breath: such a baker always has some to hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A baker of pies and tarts always keeps a supply of light flaky dough on hand.
